limits-from-plots-s1.title: The graph of $f$
limits-from-plots-s1.text: The graph of $f$ for $-4 \le x \le 4$ has three pieces. A line rises from $(-4, 1)$ to an open circle at $(-2, 3)$; a filled dot sits at $(-2, 1)$. A curve leaves the open circle at $(-2, 3)$ and falls to the filled point $(1, -1.5)$. A line starts at an open circle at $(1, 0)$ and rises to $(4, 3)$.

plot.label: Graph of the piecewise function f from x = -4 to x = 4 with a hole at (-2, 3), a dot at (-2, 1) and a jump at x = 1

limits-from-plots-s2.title: The graph of $h$
limits-from-plots-s2.text: The graph of $h$ for $-2 \le x \le 6.5$ has a vertical asymptote at $x = 3$ (dashed). To the left of 3 the graph falls without bound; to the right it rises without bound. There is an open circle at $(1, 1)$ and a filled dot at $(1, 4)$. The graph passes through $(5, 3)$.

plot.label: Graph of h with a vertical asymptote at x = 3, an open circle at (1, 1) and a filled dot at (1, 4)

items.q: Reading each side of the graph, what is $\lim_{x \to -2} f(x)$?
options: The limit does not exist.

why.correct: From the left, the line heads to height 3; from the right, the curve also heads to height 3. Both one-sided limits are 3, so the limit is 3. The dot at $(-2, 1)$ is $f(-2)$, which does not affect the limit.
options: Left and right both head to 3.
1 is $f(-2)$, the filled dot. A limit does not use the value at the point.
$-2$ is the input being approached.
Both sides head to the same height, 3, so the limit exists.
The limit does not exist.

why.correct: For $x$ just to the right of 1, the graph is the rising line, whose heights head to 0, the open circle at $(1, 0)$.
options: From the right, the line heads to the open circle at height 0.
$-1.5$ is where the curve on the left ends, so it is the limit from the left.
1 is the $x$-value, not a height.
A one-sided limit only needs one side to settle, and the right side heads to 0.

items.q: Which statement about $\lim_{x \to 1} f(x)$ is correct?
options: It does not exist, because $\lim_{x \to 1^-} f(x) = -1.5$ and $\lim_{x \to 1^+} f(x) = 0$.
It equals $-1.5$, because $f(1) = -1.5$.
It equals $-0.75$, halfway between the two sides.
It does not exist, because $f(1)$ is not defined.

why.correct: A two-sided limit needs both one-sided limits to be equal. From the left the heights head to $-1.5$; from the right, to 0. They differ, so the limit does not exist.
options: Names both one-sided limits and why they rule out a limit.
$f(1) = -1.5$ is a value; it does not make the right side agree.
There is no averaging: when the sides disagree there is no limit.
$f(1)$ is defined: the filled point $(1, -1.5)$. The reason is the unequal sides.

why.correct: From the left of 1, the curve heads to $-1.5$, and the filled point at the end of that curve says $f(1) = -1.5$. They match.
options: Both equal $-1.5$.
From the right the heights head to 0, but $f(1) = -1.5$.
The limit at $-2$ is 3, but $f(-2) = 1$.
From the left of $-2$, the line heads to 3, not to the dot at 1.

mistakes.why: $f(-2)$ is the filled dot at height 1, not the open circle at height 3. The sum is $3 + 1$.
From the left, the line heads to the open circle at height 3; the dot at 1 is only the value $f(-2)$.

why.correct: From the left, the line's heights head to 3. The value $f(-2)$ is the filled dot, 1. Sum: $3 + 1 = 4$.

options: The limit does not exist.

why.correct: From both sides of $x = 1$ the curve heads to the open circle at height 1. The filled dot at $(1, 4)$ is $h(1)$, which the limit ignores.
options: Both sides head to the open circle at height 1.
4 is the value $h(1)$, not the limit.
2 is the height the curve levels toward far away, not near $x = 1$.
Both sides agree at 1, so the limit exists.
It does not exist: $h(x)$ decreases without bound as $x \to 3^-$.
It is 0, where the asymptote crosses the $x$-axis.
It is 3, the location of the asymptote.
It does not exist: $h(x)$ increases without bound as $x \to 3^-$.

why.correct: Just to the left of $x = 3$ the graph plunges downward along the asymptote, with no bottom. The outputs do not close in on any number, so this one-sided limit does not exist.
options: The left branch falls without bound.
The heights near the asymptote are huge negative numbers, not near 0.
3 is the $x$-value approached; the heights do not settle anywhere.
The left branch goes down, not up; it is the right branch that rises.

items.q: Which is the best justification that $\lim_{x \to 3} h(x)$ does not exist?
options: As $x \to 3^-$, $h(x)$ decreases without bound, and as $x \to 3^+$, $h(x)$ increases without bound, so $h(x)$ does not approach a number.
$h(3)$ is not defined, so there is no limit.
The graph has an open circle at $x = 1$.
The two sides of the graph stay off the line $x = 3$.

why.correct: The reason must be about the outputs near 3: they are unbounded on both sides (in opposite directions), so they close in on no single number.
options: Describes the outputs on each side and concludes correctly.
A missing value never decides a limit: at a hole the limit exists even though the function has no value there. Here the reason is the unbounded outputs near 3.
What happens at $x = 1$ says nothing about $x = 3$.
Not touching the asymptote is not the reason; unbounded outputs are.
The limit does not exist.

why.correct: Near $x = 5$ the graph is an unbroken curve through $(5, 3)$, so the heights close in on 3.
options: The curve passes through $(5, 3)$ with no break.
5 is the $x$-value approached.
2 is where the curve levels off far to the right, not its height at 5.
Nothing unusual happens at $x = 5$; both sides head to 3.

items.q: Near $x = 0$, the graph of a function $q$ wiggles up and down between heights $-1$ and $1$ infinitely many times, faster and faster as $x$ gets closer to 0. What is $\lim_{x \to 0} q(x)$?
options: It does not exist, because the outputs oscillate and settle on no single number.
$0$, the height halfway between $-1$ and $1$.
$1$, the highest height the graph reaches.
It does not exist, because the outputs grow without bound.

why.correct: However close $x$ gets to 0, the outputs keep taking every value from $-1$ to 1. They never settle near one number, so there is no limit.
options: Oscillating outputs settle on nothing.
The outputs pass through 0 but never stay close to it.
The graph keeps coming back down from 1.
The outputs stay between $-1$ and 1; they are bounded. The cause is oscillation.

items.q: For a function $p$, $\lim_{x \to 4^-} p(x) = 7$, $\lim_{x \to 4^+} p(x) = 7$ and $p(4) = 2$. What is $\lim_{x \to 4} p(x)$?
options: The limit does not exist.

why.correct: Both one-sided limits are 7, so the two-sided limit is 7. The value $p(4) = 2$ does not change that.
options: Equal one-sided limits give the limit.
2 is the value at 4; the limit ignores it.
Limits are not averages of the value and the trend.
The one-sided limits agree, so the limit exists.

items.q: Which condition guarantees that $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = 5$?
options: $\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = 5$ and $\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = 5$
$\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = 5$
$f(a) = 5$ and $\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = 5$

why.correct: A two-sided limit exists and equals $L$ exactly when both one-sided limits exist and equal $L$.
options: Both sides equal 5: that is the definition's test.
The value at $a$ says nothing about nearby outputs.
One side is not enough; the right side could head elsewhere.
The right side is still unknown, and the value does not help.

items.q: A graph has an open circle at $(2, 5)$, a filled dot at $(2, 1)$, and the curve heads to the open circle from the left and from the right. Which statements are both true?
options: $\lim_{x \to 2^-} f(x) = 5$ and $\lim_{x \to 2^+} f(x) = 1$

why.correct: The curve on both sides heads to the open circle, so the limit is 5. The filled dot is the value: $f(2) = 1$.
options: Limit from the curve, value from the dot.
The two numbers are swapped.
The open circle is not the value; the filled dot is.
Both sides of the curve head to 5; the dot is not a one-sided limit.

items.q: On a graphing calculator at the standard zoom, the graph of $r(x) = \frac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}$ looks like an unbroken straight line through $(2, 4)$. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The picture suggests $\lim_{x \to 2} r(x) = 4$, but $r(2)$ is not defined, so the hole is too small to see at this scale.
$r(2) = 4$, because the graph shows a point there.
The limit at 2 does not exist, because $r(2)$ is not defined.
The graph proves the limit is 4 with no further work needed.

why.correct: A screen draws in pixels, so a single missing point is invisible. Scale can hide behavior. The graph suggests the limit is 4, while the formula shows $x = 2$ makes the denominator 0, so $r(2)$ does not exist.
options: The graph suggests 4; the formula shows the hole.
Substituting $x = 2$ gives a zero denominator, so there is no value at 2.
A missing value does not prevent a limit.
A picture suggests; it cannot show a hole one point wide.

items.q: Let $f(x) = \begin{cases} x + 1 & x < 2 \\ 7 & x = 2 \\ 5 - x & x > 2 \end{cases}$. Find $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$.

mistakes.why: 7 is $f(2)$. The limit uses the pieces for $x$ near 2: from the left $x + 1 \to 3$, from the right $5 - x \to 3$.

why.correct: From the left, $x + 1$ heads to 3. From the right, $5 - x$ heads to 3. Both one-sided limits are 3, so $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 3$, even though $f(2) = 7$.

items.q: Which graph feature matches $\lim_{x \to 1^-} g(x) = 2$, $\lim_{x \to 1^+} g(x) = 2$ and $g(1)$ not defined?
options: A hole at $(1, 2)$ with no dot above or below it
A filled dot at $(1, 2)$ on an unbroken curve
A jump at $x = 1$ from height 2 to another height
A vertical asymptote at $x = 1$

why.correct: Both sides head to height 2, and there is no value at $x = 1$: a hole at $(1, 2)$.
options: Both sides head to 2 and nothing is plotted at $x = 1$.
A filled dot would mean $g(1) = 2$ is defined.
A jump would make the one-sided limits differ.
An asymptote means unbounded outputs, not outputs heading to 2.
